meta.title: Who really said "A teacher, a really good sensei, is never a giver of 'truth'; he is a guide, a pointer to the truth that the student must discover for himself"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Bruce Lee really wrote it — in his essay "Liberate Yourself from Classical Karate," Black Belt magazine, September 1971, page 27. The popular version is trimmed.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A teacher, a really good sensei, is never a giver of 'truth'; he is a guide, a pointer to the truth that the student must discover for himself'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Bruce Lee — from his signed Black Belt essay of September 1971. But the version you've seen drops "sensei" and rewrites the ending.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1940–1973 · Martial artist, actor and founder of Jeet Kune Do
answer.sourceLine: Genuine, and unusually well documented for a Bruce Lee line. He wrote it under his own byline in “Liberate Yourself from Classical Karate,” his essay in Black Belt magazine, September 1971 — the quotation falls on page 27. Quote Investigator ↗ traces the wording to that issue, and the popular version you usually see is a trimmed edit of it.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Black Belt, vol. 9, no. 9 (September 1971), Black Belt, Inc., Los Angeles
Bruce Lee — essay starts p. 24; quotation on p. 27, col. 2
Written in English — no translation involved

source.excerpt: A teacher, a really good sensei, is never a giver of ‘truth’; he is a guide, a pointer to the truth that the student must discover for himself. A good teacher, therefore, studies each student individually and encourages the student to explore himself, both internally and externally.
trail: September 1971 — Black Belt vol. 9, no. 9 carries Lee’s essay “Liberate Yourself from Classical Karate,” starting p. 24. The sentence appears on p. 27, col. 2, in the wording quoted here — Quote Investigator’s earliest citation ↗. The issue is scanned at the Internet Archive ↗.
December 1988 — Black Belt reprints the essay (vol. 26, no. 12) with the text altered: “pointer” becomes “pioneer,” and the “sensei” phrasing is gone, per QI ↗.
2001 — John R. Little’s Bruce Lee: Artist of Life prints yet another form on p. 141, with “a really good teacher” for “a really good sensei” — also catalogued by QI ↗.
Today — the version that spreads is shorter still, source-free, and carried on aggregators with no citation ↗. The full essay text, including this paragraph, is transcribed online ↗.
source.excerptNote: The preceding paragraphs of the essay attack the “sensei” and “masters” whose drills, in Lee’s account, make the student lose sight of the end — which is what gives the word “sensei” its edge here.

author.metaLine: 1940–1973 · Martial artist, actor, filmmaker and founder of Jeet Kune Do
author.bio: Bruce Lee was born in San Francisco on 27 November 1940 and died in Hong Kong on 20 July 1973, aged 32. Best known as an actor and martial artist, he was also a working writer: he founded the hybrid martial-arts philosophy Jeet Kune Do in 1967 and argued for it in print as well as on film. His September 1971 Black Belt essay “Liberate Yourself from Classical Karate” is one of the few pieces of martial-arts philosophy he published under his own byline during his lifetime — which is why quotes drawn from it, unlike most sayings pinned to his name, can actually be checked.

misattribution.heading: Right author, wrong wording
misattribution.intro: This one is not a fake. The problem is that almost nobody quotes it correctly, and almost nobody cites it at all — and two of the three corrupted versions were published by Bruce Lee’s own publishers.

items.why: The form that dominates quote sites reads “A teacher is never a giver of truth; he is a guide, a pointer to the truth that each student must find for himself” — dropping “a really good sensei” and rewriting “the student must discover for himself.” It circulates with no source attached at all ↗.
When Black Belt reran the essay in December 1988, the text had changed: “pointer” became “pioneer,” and the “sensei” phrasing was deleted, per Quote Investigator ↗.
John R. Little’s compilation prints a third form — “A teacher, a really good teacher, is never a giver of truth; he is a guide, a pointer to truth” — on page 141, as documented by QI ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The wording asked about here is the 1971 original: Bruce Lee, “Liberate Yourself from Classical Karate,” Black Belt, September 1971, page 27 — the version Quote Investigator judges the most accurate ↗.

context.heading: Why he wrote it
lead: The sentence is the constructive half of an argument. In the same essay Lee spends several paragraphs attacking what he calls the “sensei” and “masters” of classical training — teachers whose elaborate drills, he says, absorb so much of the student’s attention that the student loses sight of the end, and ends up reciting circumstances rather than responding to them. Having demolished the bad teacher, he then defines the good one, and pointedly keeps the word sensei: a really good sensei is not a dispenser of answers but a finger pointing somewhere the student has to walk himself.

Lee follows the line by describing what that looks like in practice — studying each student individually, encouraging self-exploration, and, in his phrase, being a catalyst. The essay was his public manifesto for Jeet Kune Do and provoked a wide reaction in traditional martial-arts circles. He published it in September 1971, less than two years before his death in July 1973.
detailsBody: Three published versions circulate, all bearing Bruce Lee’s name. The 1971 original is the one quoted here. Black Belt’s own December 1988 reprint of the essay altered it — “pointer” became “pioneer” and the “sensei” phrasing was dropped. John R. Little’s 2001 compilation Bruce Lee: Artist of Life prints a third form, with “a really good teacher” in place of “a really good sensei.”

Quote Investigator’s judgement is that the 1971 text is the most accurate, while noting that magazine editing sometimes produces revisions. That makes this an unusual case: the corruption of the quote did not start with the internet: it started with the magazine that first printed it.
context.pull: He kept the word sensei in the sentence deliberately — the paragraph just above it is an attack on the bad ones.
